claim: Osteolectin/Clec11a is required to maintain adult skeletal bone mass.
source: We previously discovered a new osteogenic growth factor that is required to maintain adult skeletal bone mass, Osteolectin/Clec11a.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a previously established finding from prior work.

claim: Osteolectin acts on Leptin Receptor+ (LepR+) skeletal stem cells and other osteogenic progenitors in bone marrow to promote their differentiation into osteoblasts.
source: Osteolectin acts on Leptin Receptor+ (LepR+) skeletal stem cells and other osteogenic progenitors in bone marrow to promote their differentiation into osteoblasts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a previously established finding.

claim: Integrin α11 is a receptor for Osteolectin.
source: Here we identify a receptor for Osteolectin, integrin α11, which is expressed by LepR+ cells and osteoblasts.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments including binding assays and functional studies.

claim: Integrin α11 is expressed by LepR+ cells and osteoblasts.
source: Here we identify a receptor for Osteolectin, integrin α11, which is expressed by LepR+ cells and osteoblasts.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1.

claim: α11β1 integrin binds Osteolectin with nanomolar affinity.
source: α11β1 integrin binds Osteolectin with nanomolar affinity and is required for the osteogenic response to Osteolectin.
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data showing kd of 0.3 nM (Figure 1I and J).

claim: Integrin α11 is required for the osteogenic response to Osteolectin.
source: α11β1 integrin binds Osteolectin with nanomolar affinity and is required for the osteogenic response to Osteolectin.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that deletion of Itga11 blocks osteogenic differentiation in response to Osteolectin (Figure 4).

claim: Deletion of Itga11 from mouse and human bone marrow stromal cells impaired osteogenic differentiation.
source: Deletion of Itga11 (which encodes α11) from mouse and human bone marrow stromal cells impaired osteogenic differentiation and blocked their response to Osteolectin.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro differentiation assays shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Deletion of Itga11 from mouse and human bone marrow stromal cells blocked their response to Osteolectin.
source: Deletion of Itga11 (which encodes α11) from mouse and human bone marrow stromal cells impaired osteogenic differentiation and blocked their response to Osteolectin.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing no osteogenic response to Osteolectin in Itga11-deficient cells (Figure 4A, B, and Figure 7F, G).

claim: Lepr-cre; Itga11fl/fl mice appeared grossly normal.
source: Like Osteolectin deficient mice, Lepr-cre; Itga11fl/fl mice appeared grossly normal but exhibited reduced osteogenesis and accelerated bone loss during adulthood.
evidence: This is supported by observations of body length, body mass, and femur length (Figure 5A-D).

claim: Lepr-cre; Itga11fl/fl mice exhibited reduced osteogenesis during adulthood.
source: Like Osteolectin deficient mice, Lepr-cre; Itga11fl/fl mice appeared grossly normal but exhibited reduced osteogenesis and accelerated bone loss during adulthood.
evidence: This is supported by reduced mineral apposition rate and P1NP levels (Figure 5M and O).

claim: Lepr-cre; Itga11fl/fl mice exhibited accelerated bone loss during adulthood.
source: Like Osteolectin deficient mice, Lepr-cre; Itga11fl/fl mice appeared grossly normal but exhibited reduced osteogenesis and accelerated bone loss during adulthood.
evidence: This is supported by microCT analysis showing reduced trabecular bone volume at 6 and 12 months (Figure 5F-L).

claim: Osteolectin binding to α11β1 promoted Wnt pathway activation.
source: Osteolectin binding to α11β1 promoted Wnt pathway activation, which was necessary for the osteogenic response to Osteolectin.
evidence: This is supported by Western blots showing increased GSK3 phosphorylation and β-catenin levels (Figure 2D, E) and increased Wnt target gene expression (Figure 2F).

claim: Wnt pathway activation was necessary for the osteogenic response to Osteolectin.
source: Osteolectin binding to α11β1 promoted Wnt pathway activation, which was necessary for the osteogenic response to Osteolectin.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that the β-catenin inhibitor IWR-1-endo blocked the osteogenic effect of Osteolectin (Figure 3C and D).

claim: Human and mouse Osteolectin contain RGD and LDT integrin-binding motifs.
source: To generate hypotheses regarding potential Osteolectin receptors, we examined the amino acid sequence and found two integrin-binding motifs, RGD (Gardner and Hynes, 1985; Pierschbacher and Ruoslahti, 1984; Plow et al., 1985) and LDT (Fong et al., 1997; Viney et al., 1996) in human (Figure 1A) and mouse Osteolectin (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by amino acid sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A and B, with citations to prior work on integrin-binding motifs.

claim: The RGD and LDT domains are evolutionarily conserved among bony vertebrates.
source: One or both of these motifs were conserved across Osteolectin sequences in all bony vertebrates (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Itga11 was highly expressed by LepR+CD45-Ter119-CD31- stromal cells and Col2.3-GFP+CD45-Ter119-CD31- osteoblasts but not by any hematopoietic stem or progenitor population.
source: Quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis of sorted bone marrow cells (Supplementary file 1 shows the markers used to isolate these cells) showed that Itga11 was highly expressed by LepR+CD45-Ter119-CD31- stromal cells and Col2.3-GFP+CD45-Ter119-CD31- osteoblasts but not by any hematopoietic stem or progenitor population (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Anti-Flag antibody co-immunoprecipitated endogenous integrin β1 and integrin α11 with Flag-tagged Osteolectin in MC3T3-E1 preosteoblast cells.
source: In MC3T3-E1 preosteoblast cells expressing Flag-tagged Osteolectin, anti-Flag antibody co-immunoprecipitated endogenous integrin β1 and integrin α11 with Flag-tagged Osteolectin (results are representative of two independent experiments).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Recombinant human Osteolectin selectively bound to recombinant human integrin α11β1 and α10β1, but not to other integrins.
source: Recombinant human Osteolectin (rhOln) selectively bound to recombinant human integrin α11β1 and α10β1, but not to other integrins (n = 3 independent experiments).
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Integrin α11β1 bound Osteolectin and recombinant human Pro-Collagen 1α with similar affinities, but not bovine serum albumin (BSA).
source: Integrin α11β1 bound Osteolectin and recombinant human Pro-Collagen 1α (rhCol1A) with similar affinities, but not bovine serum albumin (BSA) (n = 3 independent experiments).
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Osteolectin, but not Pro-Collagen 1α, promoted osteogenic differentiation by MC3T3-E1 cells and human bone marrow stromal cells.
source: Osteolectin, but not Pro-Collagen 1α, promoted osteogenic differentiation by MC3T3-E1 cells and human bone marrow stromal cells (n = 3 independent experiments).
evidence: This is supported by Alizarin red staining data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: 200 nM RGDS peptide inhibited the binding of integrin α11β1 to recombinant human Osteolectin.
source: 200 nM RGDS peptide inhibited the binding of integrin α11β1 to recombinant human Osteolectin.
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: 100 μM RGDS peptide inhibited osteogenic differentiation by MC3T3-E1 cells and human bone marrow stromal cells in response to 30 ng/ml of recombinant human Osteolectin.
source: 100 μM RGDS peptide inhibited osteogenic differentiation by MC3T3-E1 cells and human bone marrow stromal cells in response to 30 ng/ml of recombinant human Osteolectin.
evidence: This is supported by Alizarin red staining data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells secrete Osteolectin into the culture medium.
source: MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells secrete Osteolectin into the culture medium (Figure 2A), consistent with our observation that Osteolectin is synthesized by a subset of LepR+ bone marrow stromal cells (Yue et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Deletion of Osteolectin from MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells reduced their osteogenic differentiation in osteogenic differentiation medium.
source: Deletion of Osteolectin from these cell lines reduced their osteogenic differentiation in osteogenic differentiation medium (Figure 2B and C), demonstrating that autocrine Osteolectin production is part of what drives osteogenesis by these cells in culture.
evidence: This is supported by Alizarin red staining and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Autocrine Osteolectin production is part of what drives osteogenesis by MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells in culture.
source: Deletion of Osteolectin from these cell lines reduced their osteogenic differentiation in osteogenic differentiation medium (Figure 2B and C), demonstrating that autocrine Osteolectin production is part of what drives osteogenesis by these cells in culture.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of Osteolectin reduces osteogenic differentiation.

claim: Osteolectin treatment dramatically increased GSK3 phosphorylation at Ser21/9 within 30 to 60 min in MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells.
source: The most prominent change we observed was a dramatic increase of GSK3 phosphorylation at Ser21/9 within 30 to 60 min of Osteolectin treatment in all three cell lines (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Osteolectin treatment increased β-catenin levels within 24 hr in MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells.
source: We did not observe an increase in β-catenin levels within 1 hr of Osteolectin treatment, but did detect increased β-catenin levels in all three cell lines within 24 hr of Osteolectin treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The transcription of Wnt target genes Axin2, Lef1, Runx2, and Alkaline phosphatase were activated within 24 hr of Osteolectin treatment.
source: The transcription of several Wnt target genes, including Axin2 (Jho et al., 2002; Lustig et al., 2002; Yan et al., 2001; Yan et al., 2009), Lef1 (Filali et al., 2002; Gaur et al., 2005; Hovanes et al., 2001), Runx2 (Dong et al., 2006; Gaur et al., 2005), and Alkaline phosphatase (Rawadi et al., 2003), were activated within 24 hr of Osteolectin treatment (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2F, with citations to prior work identifying these as Wnt target genes.

claim: Osteolectin deficient MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells had lower levels of phospho-GSK3 and β-catenin as compared to parental cells.
source: Osteolectin deficient MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells had lower levels of phospho-GSK3 and β-catenin as compared to parental cells (Figure 2G) as well as significantly lower levels of Wnt target genes (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Osteolectin deficient MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells had significantly lower levels of Wnt target genes as compared to parental cells.
source: Osteolectin deficient MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells had lower levels of phospho-GSK3 and β-catenin as compared to parental cells (Figure 2G) as well as significantly lower levels of Wnt target genes (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Osteolectin promotes Wnt pathway activation in osteogenic cells.
source: These data demonstrate that Osteolectin promotes Wnt pathway activation in osteogenic cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing increased GSK3 phosphorylation, β-catenin levels, and Wnt target gene expression.

claim: AZD2858 increased GSK3 phosphorylation and β-catenin levels in MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells.
source: As expected (Gilmour et al., 2013; Marsell et al., 2012; Sisask et al., 2013), AZD2858 increased GSK3 phosphorylation and β-catenin levels (Figure 3A) as well as osteogenic differentiation (Figure 3B) by MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A, with citations to prior work on AZD2858.

claim: AZD2858 increased osteogenic differentiation by MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells.
source: As expected (Gilmour et al., 2013; Marsell et al., 2012; Sisask et al., 2013), AZD2858 increased GSK3 phosphorylation and β-catenin levels (Figure 3A) as well as osteogenic differentiation (Figure 3B) by MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells.
evidence: This is supported by Alizarin red staining data shown in Figure 3B, with citations to prior work on AZD2858.

claim: When Osteolectin and AZD2858 were added together, there was no further promotion of osteogenic differentiation beyond the effects of the individual agents.
source: However, when the two agents were added together, there was no further promotion of osteogenic differentiation beyond the effects of the individual agents (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Alizarin red staining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Osteolectin and GSK3/β-catenin act in the same pathway to promote osteogenic differentiation by mesenchymal progenitors.
source: These data suggest that Osteolectin and GSK3/β-catenin act in the same pathway to promote osteogenic differentiation by mesenchymal progenitors.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that combining Osteolectin and AZD2858 does not have an additive effect.

claim: IWR-1-endo reduced β-catenin levels and osteogenesis in MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells.
source: As expected, Osteolectin increased β-catenin levels and osteogenesis by MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells while IWR-1-endo reduced β-catenin levels and osteogenesis (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and Alizarin red staining data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: IWR-1-endo blocked the effect of Osteolectin on β-catenin levels and osteogenesis when added together.
source: When added together, IWR-1-endo blocked the effect of Osteolectin on β-catenin levels and osteogenesis (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and Alizarin red staining data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Osteolectin requires β-catenin to induce osteogenesis by mesenchymal progenitors.
source: This suggests that Osteolectin requires β-catenin to induce osteogenesis by mesenchymal progenitors.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that IWR-1-endo blocks the osteogenic effect of Osteolectin.

claim: Deletion of Itga11 significantly reduced osteogenesis by MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells in culture.
source: Deletion of Itga11 significantly reduced osteogenesis by each cell line in culture (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by Alizarin red staining and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Addition of recombinant Osteolectin to culture significantly promoted osteogenesis by parental, but not Itga11 deficient, MC3T3-E1, hBMSC#1, and hBMSC#2 cells.
source: Addition of recombinant Osteolectin to culture significantly promoted osteogenesis by parental, but not Itga11 deficient, MC3T3-E1, hBMSC#1, and hBMSC#2 cells (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by Alizarin red staining and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Integrin α11 is required by mouse pre-osteoblast cells and human bone marrow stromal cells to undergo osteogenesis in response to Osteolectin.
source: Integrin α11 is therefore required by mouse pre-osteoblast cells and human bone marrow stromal cells to undergo osteogenesis in response to Osteolectin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Itga11-deficient cells do not respond to Osteolectin.

claim: Itga11 deficient MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells exhibited lower levels of GSK3 phosphorylation and β-catenin as compared to parental control cells.
source: The Itga11 deficient MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells also exhibited lower levels of GSK3 phosphorylation and β-catenin as compared to parental control cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Addition of recombinant Osteolectin to culture increased the levels of phosphorylated GSK3 and β-catenin in parental control cells but not in Itga11 deficient cells.
source: Addition of recombinant Osteolectin to culture increased the levels of phosphorylated GSK3 and β-catenin in parental control cells but not in Itga11 deficient cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Itga11 deficient cells had significantly lower levels of Wnt target gene transcripts.
source: We also observed significantly lower levels of Wnt target gene transcripts in the Itga11 deficient cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Addition of recombinant Osteolectin to culture significantly increased the levels of Wnt target gene transcripts in parental control cells but not in Itga11 deficient cells.
source: Addition of recombinant Osteolectin to culture significantly increased the levels of Wnt target gene transcripts in parental control cells but not in Itga11 deficient cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Integrin α11 is required by mouse pre-osteoblast cells and human bone marrow stromal cells to activate Wnt pathway signaling in response to Osteolectin.
source: Integrin α11 is therefore required by mouse pre-osteoblast cells and human bone marrow stromal cells to activate Wnt pathway signaling in response to Osteolectin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Itga11-deficient cells do not show Wnt pathway activation in response to Osteolectin.

claim: Addition of Pro-Collagen 1α to MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells did not affect the levels of phosphorylated GSK3, β-catenin, or Wnt target gene transcripts.
source: Addition of recombinant Osteolectin to culture increased levels of phosphorylated GSK3, β-catenin, and Wnt target gene transcripts in MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, and hBMSC#2 cells (Figure 4E and F); however, addition of Pro-Collagen 1α to these cells did not seem to have any effect on the levels of phosphorylated GSK3, β-catenin, or Wnt target gene transcripts in these cells (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Both Pro-Collagen 1α and Osteolectin promoted Focal Adhesion Kinase (FAK) phosphorylation at Tyrosine 397 within one hour of addition to primary mouse bone marrow stromal cells in culture.
source: Both Pro-Collagen 1α and Osteolectin promoted Focal Adhesion Kinase (FAK) phosphorylation at Tyrosine 397 within one hour of addition to culture without affecting total FAK levels (Figure 4G), consistent with the activation of integrin signaling (Cooper et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4G, with citation to prior work on FAK phosphorylation and integrin signaling.

claim: Pro-Collagen 1α increased the levels of phosphorylated GSK3 in primary mouse bone marrow stromal cells.
source: Although Pro-Collagen 1α had not detectably affected GSK3 phosphorylation in MC3T3-E1 cells, hBMSC#1 cells, or hBMSC#2 cells (Figure 4E), it did increase the levels of phosphorylated GSK3 in primary mouse bone marrow stromal cells, as did Osteolectin (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Osteolectin, but not Pro-Collagen 1α, promoted β-catenin accumulation within 24 hr of treatment in primary mouse bone marrow stromal cells.
source: Osteolectin, but not Pro-Collagen 1α, promoted β-catenin accumulation within 24 hr of treatment (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Osteolectin treatment increased nuclear β-catenin within 4 hr of treatment in primary mouse bone marrow stromal cells.
source: Osteolectin treatment did not significantly affect the levels of cytosolic/membrane associated β-catenin at any time point, but did increase nuclear β-catenin within 4 hr of treatment (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data of nuclear and cytosolic fractions shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Osteolectin treatment did not significantly affect Ctnnb1 transcript levels in primary mouse bone marrow stromal cells.
source: Osteolectin treatment did not significantly affect Ctnnb1 (which encodes β-catenin) transcript levels in these cells (Figure 4J), suggesting that the increase in nuclear β-catenin reflected an inhibition of proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The increase in nuclear β-catenin in response to Osteolectin reflected an inhibition of proteasomal degradation.
source: Osteolectin treatment did not significantly affect Ctnnb1 (which encodes β-catenin) transcript levels in these cells (Figure 4J), suggesting that the increase in nuclear β-catenin reflected an inhibition of proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that β-catenin protein levels increased without a change in transcript levels.

claim: Osteolectin promoted integrin α11 signaling, leading to Wnt pathway activation, accumulation of nuclear β-catenin, and increased transcription of Wnt target genes involved in osteogenesis.
source: Together, these data suggest that Osteolectin promoted integrin α11 signaling, leading to Wnt pathway activation, accumulation of nuclear β-catenin, and increased transcription of Wnt target genes involved in osteogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing the signaling cascade.

claim: Itga11-deficiency blocked the ability of Osteolectin to promote FAK phosphorylation in primary bone marrow stromal cells.
source: Itga11-deficiency blocked the ability of Osteolectin to promote FAK phosphorylation in primary bone marrow stromal cells, but did not affect the ability of Pro-Collagen 1α to promote FAK phosphorylation (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Itga11-deficiency did not affect the ability of Pro-Collagen 1α to promote FAK phosphorylation in primary bone marrow stromal cells.
source: Itga11-deficiency blocked the ability of Osteolectin to promote FAK phosphorylation in primary bone marrow stromal cells, but did not affect the ability of Pro-Collagen 1α to promote FAK phosphorylation (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Osteolectin promotes integrin signaling in an α11-dependent manner.
source: This suggests that Osteolectin promotes integrin signaling in an α11-dependent manner but that Pro-Collagen 1α promotes integrin signaling in an α11-independent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Itga11-deficiency blocks Osteolectin-induced but not Pro-Collagen 1α-induced FAK phosphorylation.

claim: Pro-Collagen 1α promotes integrin signaling in an α11-independent manner.
source: This suggests that Osteolectin promotes integrin signaling in an α11-dependent manner but that Pro-Collagen 1α promotes integrin signaling in an α11-independent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Itga11-deficiency does not block Pro-Collagen 1α-induced FAK phosphorylation.

claim: Only 5% of osteoblasts derive from LepR+ cells at two months of age.
source: Only 5% of osteoblasts derive from LepR+ cells at two months of age but this number increases to approximately 50% by 10 months of age (Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Zhou et al., 2014).

claim: Approximately 50% of osteoblasts derive from LepR+ cells by 10 months of age.
source: Only 5% of osteoblasts derive from LepR+ cells at two months of age but this number increases to approximately 50% by 10 months of age (Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Zhou et al., 2014).

claim: Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice did not exhibit the defects in incisor development observed in germline Itga11-/- mice.
source: Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice did not exhibit the defects in incisor development (data not shown) or the growth retardation observed in germline Itga11-/- mice (Popova et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as an observation, with citation to prior work on germline Itga11-/- mice.

claim: Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice did not exhibit the growth retardation observed in germline Itga11-/- mice.
source: Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice did not exhibit the defects in incisor development (data not shown) or the growth retardation observed in germline Itga11-/- mice (Popova et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as an observation, with citation to prior work on germline Itga11-/- mice.

claim: Body lengths did not significantly differ between Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice and sex-matched littermate controls at 2, 6, or 12 months of age.
source: Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice appeared grossly normal (Figure 5A), with body lengths (Figure 5B), body masses (Figure 5C), and femur lengths (Figure 5D) that did not significantly differ from sex-matched littermate controls.
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Body masses did not significantly differ between Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice and sex-matched littermate controls at 2, 6, or 12 months of age.
source: Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice appeared grossly normal (Figure 5A), with body lengths (Figure 5B), body masses (Figure 5C), and femur lengths (Figure 5D) that did not significantly differ from sex-matched littermate controls.
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Femur lengths did not significantly differ between Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice and sex-matched littermate controls at 2, 6, or 12 months of age.
source: Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice appeared grossly normal (Figure 5A), with body lengths (Figure 5B), body masses (Figure 5C), and femur lengths (Figure 5D) that did not significantly differ from sex-matched littermate controls.
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: LepR+ bone marrow cells from Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice had an approximately 85% reduction in Itga11 transcript levels as compared to LepR+ cells from control mice.
source: However, qRT-PCR analysis showed that LepR+ bone marrow cells from Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice had an approximately 85% reduction in Itga11 transcript levels as compared to LepR+ cells from control mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Serum Osteolectin levels did not significantly differ between Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice and littermate controls at 2 or 12 months of age.
source: Serum Osteolectin levels did not significantly differ between Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice and littermate controls at 2 or 12 months of age but were modestly higher in Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice than in controls at 6 months of age (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Serum Osteolectin levels were modestly higher in Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice than in controls at 6 months of age.
source: Serum Osteolectin levels did not significantly differ between Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice and littermate controls at 2 or 12 months of age but were modestly higher in Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice than in controls at 6 months of age (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Integrin α11 is not required for the synthesis or secretion of Osteolectin.
source: This demonstrates that Integrin α11 is not required for the synthesis or secretion of Osteolectin.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that serum Osteolectin levels are not reduced in Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice.

claim: No significant difference in trabecular bone parameters was observed between Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice and sex-matched littermates at 2 months of age.
source: Consistent with the observation that LepR+ cells contribute little to skeletal development prior to 2 months of age (Zhou et al., 2014), we observed no significant difference in trabecular bone parameters between Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice and sex-matched littermates at 2 months of age (Figure 5F–L).
evidence: This is supported by microCT data shown in Figure 5F-L, with citation to prior work on LepR+ cell contribution.

claim: 6 and 12-month-old male and female Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice had significantly reduced trabecular bone volume as compared to sex-matched littermate controls.
source: However, LepR+ cells and Osteolectin are necessary for adult osteogenesis (Yue et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2014). Consistent with this, 6 and 12-month-old male and female Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice had significantly reduced trabecular bone volume as compared to sex-matched littermate controls (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is supported by microCT data shown in Figure 5F and G, with citations to prior work.

claim: At 6 and 12 months of age, male and female Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice tended to have lower trabecular number and trabecular thickness than sex matched littermate controls.
source: At 6 and 12 months of age, male and female Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice also tended to have lower trabecular number (Figure 5H) and trabecular thickness (Figure 5I) than sex matched littermate controls.
evidence: This is supported by microCT data shown in Figure 5H and I.

claim: The mineral apposition rate was significantly reduced in trabecular bone from Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice as compared to sex-matched littermates at 6 and 12 months of age.
source: Calcein double labelling showed that the mineral apposition rate was significantly reduced in trabecular bone from Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice as compared to sex-matched littermates at 6 and 12 months of age (Figure 5M).
evidence: This is supported by calcein double labeling data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Levels of Procollagen type 1 N-terminal Propeptide (P1NP) were significantly lower in the serum of Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice as compared to littermate controls at 6 and 12 months of age.
source: Levels of Procollagen type 1 N-terminal Propeptide (P1NP), a marker of bone formation, were also significantly lower in the serum of Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice as compared to littermate controls at 6 and 12 months of age (Figure 5O).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5O.

claim: Integrin α11 is required by LepR+ cells and their progeny for normal rates of trabecular bone formation and maintenance of trabecular bone volume during adulthood.
source: Integrin α11 is, therefore, required by LepR+ cells and their progeny for normal rates of trabecular bone formation and maintenance of trabecular bone volume during adulthood, phenocopying the accelerated trabecular bone loss in adult Osteolectin deficient mice (Yue et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the bone formation and bone volume data, with citation to prior work on Osteolectin deficient mice.

claim: Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice did not significantly differ from sex-matched littermates in the urinary bone resorption marker deoxypyridinoline at 6 or 12 months of age.
source: While Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice had significantly reduced rates of bone formation as compared to sex-matched littermates (Figure 5M), they did not significantly differ in the urinary bone resorption marker deoxypyridinoline at 6 or 12 months of age (Figure 5N; this was not tested in 2-month-old mice because no difference in bone parameters was observed at that age).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5N.

claim: Like Osteolectin, Integrin α11 promotes bone formation but does not regulate bone resorption.
source: This suggests that, like Osteolectin, Integrin α11 promotes bone formation but does not regulate bone resorption (Yue et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that bone formation is reduced but bone resorption is not affected, with citation to prior work on Osteolectin.

claim: Osteolectin deficiency has a milder effect on cortical bone as compared to trabecular bone, with no significant reduction in cortical bone until after 10 months of age.
source: Osteolectin deficiency has a milder effect on cortical bone as compared to trabecular bone, with no significant reduction in cortical bone until after 10 months of age (Yue et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior work (Yue et al., 2016).

claim: Femur cortical bone parameters did not significantly differ between Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice and sex-matched littermates at 2 or 6 month of age.
source: Consistent with this, femur cortical bone parameters did not significantly differ between Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice and sex-matched littermates at 2 or 6 month of age (Figure 6A–F).
evidence: This is supported by microCT data shown in Figure 6A-F.

claim: Cortical bone mineral density was significantly lower in male and female Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice as compared to sex-matched littermates at 12 months of age.
source: However, cortical bone mineral density was significantly lower in male and female Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice as compared to sex-matched littermates at 12 months of age (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by microCT data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The mineral apposition rate was significantly reduced in cortical bone from male and female Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice as compared to sex-matched littermate controls at 6 and 12 months of age.
source: Calcein double labelling revealed that the mineral apposition rate was significantly reduced in cortical bone from male and female Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice as compared to sex-matched littermate controls at 6 and 12 months of age (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by calcein double labeling data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Deletion of Integrin α11 from LepR+ cells reduces the rate of cortical bone formation during adulthood, slowly leading to a thinning of cortical bone that became apparent in the femurs at 12 months of age.
source: Deletion of Integrin α11 from LepR+ cells thus reduces the rate of cortical bone formation during adulthood, slowly leading to a thinning of cortical bone that became apparent in the femurs at 12 months of age, phenocopying the slow loss of cortical bone in adult Osteolectin deficient mice (Yue et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cortical bone data, with citation to prior work on Osteolectin deficient mice.

claim: A slight, but statistically significant, reduction in the frequency of cells that formed CFU-F colonies was observed in Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice at 2 months of age.
source: We observed a slight, but statistically significant, reduction in the frequency of cells that formed CFU-F colonies in Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice at 2 months of age, though no significant difference was apparent at 6 months of age (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by CFU-F assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: No significant difference in the frequency of cells that formed CFU-F colonies was apparent between Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice and controls at 6 months of age.
source: We observed a slight, but statistically significant, reduction in the frequency of cells that formed CFU-F colonies in Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice at 2 months of age, though no significant difference was apparent at 6 months of age (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by CFU-F assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: No significant difference in the number of cells per CFU-F colony was observed between Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice and controls at 2 or 6 months of age.
source: We observed no significant difference in the number of cells per colony at either age (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by CFU-F assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Integrin α11 is not required for the maintenance of CFU-F in vivo or for their proliferation in vitro.
source: Integrin α11 is therefore not required for the maintenance of CFU-F in vivo or for their proliferation in vitro.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CFU-F frequency and colony size are not substantially affected by Itga11 deficiency.

claim: Bone marrow stromal cells from Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice formed significantly less bone in culture as compared to control colonies.
source: Consistent with the decreased osteogenesis from Itga11 deficient mesenchymal cell lines in culture (Figure 4A) and the reduced osteogenesis in Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice in vivo (Figure 5 and Figure 6), bone marrow stromal cells from Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice formed significantly less bone in culture as compared to control colonies (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by Alizarin red staining data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Like Osteolectin, Integrin α11 promotes osteogenesis by bone marrow stromal cells.
source: This demonstrates that, like Osteolectin, Integrin α11 promotes osteogenesis by bone marrow stromal cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Itga11-deficient bone marrow stromal cells show reduced osteogenesis.

claim: No difference was detected between Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl and control colonies in adipogenic or chondrogenic differentiation.
source: We did not detect any difference between Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl and control colonies in adipogenic or chondrogenic differentiation (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is supported by Oil red O and Toluidine blue staining data shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: Osteolectin significantly increased osteogenic differentiation by control CFU-F colonies, but Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl colonies underwent significantly less osteogenesis and did not respond to Osteolectin.
source: Osteolectin significantly increased osteogenic differentiation by control colonies, but Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl colonies underwent significantly less osteogenesis and did not respond to Osteolectin (Figure 7F and G).
evidence: This is supported by Alizarin red staining and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: Osteolectin treatment significantly increased the levels of the Wnt target gene transcripts Alp, Axin2, Lef1, and Runx2 in cells from control mice, but not Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice.
source: Osteolectin treatment also significantly increased the levels of the Wnt target gene transcripts Alp, Axin2, Lef1, and Runx2 in cells from control mice, but not Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Bone marrow stromal cells require Integrin α11 to undergo osteogenesis in response to Osteolectin.
source: Bone marrow stromal cells thus require Integrin α11 to undergo osteogenesis in response to Osteolectin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Itga11-deficient bone marrow stromal cells do not respond to Osteolectin.

claim: In the distal femur metaphysis of control mice, Osteolectin treatment significantly increased trabecular bone volume, trabecular bone number, and trabecular connectivity density, while significantly reducing trabecular spacing.
source: Consistent with our prior study (Yue et al., 2016), in the distal femur metaphysis of control mice, Osteolectin treatment significantly increased trabecular bone volume (Figure 7H and I), trabecular bone number (Figure 7J), and trabecular connectivity density (Figure 7M), while significantly reducing trabecular spacing (Figure 7L).
evidence: This is supported by microCT data shown in Figure 7H-M, with citation to prior work.

claim: Osteolectin treatment had no significant effect on trabecular bone parameters in Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice.
source: However, Osteolectin treatment had no significant effect on these parameters in Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice (Figure 7H–N).
evidence: This is supported by microCT data shown in Figure 7H-N.

claim: Osteolectin treatment significantly increased the levels of the Wnt target gene transcripts Alp, Lef1, and Runx2 in LepR+ cells isolated from the bone marrow of control mice, but not Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice.
source: Osteolectin treatment also significantly increased the levels of the Wnt target gene transcripts Alp, Lef1, and Runx2 in LepR+ cells isolated from the bone marrow of control mice, but not Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: LepR+ bone marrow stromal cells and their progeny require Integrin α11 to undergo osteogenesis in response to Osteolectin in vivo.
source: LepR+ bone marrow stromal cells and their progeny thus require Integrin α11 to undergo osteogenesis in response to Osteolectin in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo Osteolectin treatment experiment.

claim: Neither Osteolectin administration nor Itga11 deficiency had any significant effect on cortical bone parameters in the relatively short-term experiment performed in young mice.
source: Neither Osteolectin administration nor Itga11 deficiency had any significant effect on cortical bone parameters in this relatively short-term experiment performed in young mice (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: In control cultures, bone marrow stromal cells from Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice underwent significantly less osteogenesis as compared to stromal cells from control mice.
source: In control cultures, bone marrow stromal cells from Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice underwent significantly less osteogenesis as compared to stromal cells from control mice (Figure 7O).
evidence: This is supported by Alizarin red staining data shown in Figure 7O.

claim: Addition of AZD2858 significantly increased osteogenic differentiation from both Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl and control stromal cells.
source: Addition of AZD2858 significantly increased osteogenic differentiation from both Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl and control stromal cells.
evidence: This is supported by Alizarin red staining data shown in Figure 7O.

claim: In cultures treated with DMSO control, Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl stromal cells had lower levels of phosphorylated GSK3 and β-catenin as compared to control stromal cells.
source: In cultures treated with DMSO control, Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl stromal cells had lower levels of phosphorylated GSK3 and β-catenin as compared to control stromal cells (Figure 7P).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7P.

claim: AZD2858 increased the levels of phosphorylated GSK3 and β-catenin in both Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl and control stromal cells.
source: AZD2858 increased the levels of phosphorylated GSK3 and β-catenin in both Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl and control stromal cells (Figure 7P).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7P.

claim: Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl stromal cells retain the ability to undergo osteogenesis in response to Wnt pathway activation, even though they do not respond to Osteolectin.
source: Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl stromal cells thus retain the ability to undergo osteogenesis in response to Wnt pathway activation, even though they do not respond to Osteolectin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that AZD2858 rescues osteogenesis in Itga11-deficient cells.

claim: Integrin α11 is a physiologically important receptor for Osteolectin, mediating its effect on osteogenesis.
source: Our data demonstrate that integrin α11 is a physiologically important receptor for Osteolectin, mediating its effect on osteogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the data in the study.

claim: Multiple factors promote osteogenesis by activating the Wnt pathway, including Wnts, BMPs, hedgehog proteins, and parathyroid hormone.
source: Multiple factors promote osteogenesis by activating the Wnt pathway, including Wnts (Boyden et al., 2002; Cui et al., 2011; Gong et al., 2001), BMPs (Chen et al., 2007; Rawadi et al., 2003), hedgehog proteins (Mak et al., 2006), and parathyroid hormone (Bonnet et al., 2012; Kulkarni et al., 2005; Wan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Osteolectin contributes to Wnt pathway activation in osteogenic stem/progenitor cells along with other factors.
source: Our data suggest that Osteolectin contributes to Wnt pathway activation in osteogenic stem/progenitor cells along with other factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing that Osteolectin activates the Wnt pathway.

claim: Integrin α10 is expressed by chondrocytes.
source: Integrin α10 is expressed by osteoblasts and chondrocytes (Bengtsson et al., 2005; Engel et al., 2013) but only at a low level by bone marrow stromal cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Integrin α10 is expressed only at a low level by bone marrow stromal cells.
source: Integrin α10 is expressed by osteoblasts and chondrocytes (Bengtsson et al., 2005; Engel et al., 2013) but only at a low level by bone marrow stromal cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D, with citations to prior work.

claim: Osteolectin may promote the differentiation of hypertrophic chondrocytes into bone in adult mice, such as during fracture healing.
source: While we did not observe any cartilage defects in Osteolectin deficient mice (Yue et al., 2016), Osteolectin may promote the differentiation of hypertrophic chondrocytes into bone in adult mice, such as during fracture healing.
evidence: This is speculation based on the expression of Osteolectin and α10 integrin in chondrocytes.

claim: α10 integrin may mediate the effects of Osteolectin on hypertrophic chondrocytes while integrin α11 may mediate the effects of Osteolectin on skeletal stem/progenitor cells.
source: Therefore, α10 integrin may mediate the effects of Osteolectin on hypertrophic chondrocytes while integrin α11 may mediate the effects of Osteolectin on skeletal stem/progenitor cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the expression patterns and binding affinities of α10 and α11 integrins.

claim: It remains possible that osteolectin has other receptors.
source: It also remains possible that osteolectin has other receptors.
evidence: This is speculation acknowledging the possibility of additional receptors.

claim: Collagen is a known ligand for α11β1 integrin.
source: Collagen is a known ligand for α11β1 integrin (Popova et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Collagen binds to α11β1 with nanomolar affinity.
source: We found that collagen binds to α11β1 with nanomolar affinity (Figure 1J) and actives integrin signaling (Figure 4G and 4H, but we did not detect any effect of exogenous collagen on β-catenin accumulation (Figure 4F) or osteogenic differentiation (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by binding assay data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Collagen activates integrin signaling.
source: We found that collagen binds to α11β1 with nanomolar affinity (Figure 1J) and actives integrin signaling (Figure 4G and 4H, but we did not detect any effect of exogenous collagen on β-catenin accumulation (Figure 4F) or osteogenic differentiation (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing FAK phosphorylation in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Exogenous collagen does not affect β-catenin accumulation or osteogenic differentiation.
source: We found that collagen binds to α11β1 with nanomolar affinity (Figure 1J) and actives integrin signaling (Figure 4G and 4H, but we did not detect any effect of exogenous collagen on β-catenin accumulation (Figure 4F) or osteogenic differentiation (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 1K.

claim: Collagen may bind α11β1 in a way that regulates cell adhesion and migration but not osteogenic differentiation, at least in skeletal stem/progenitor cells.
source: This suggests that collagen may bind α11β1 in a way that regulates cell adhesion and migration but not osteogenic differentiation, at least in skeletal stem/progenitor cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that collagen activates integrin signaling but not osteogenesis.

claim: Endogenous collagen may bind α11β1 differently than exogenous collagen, potentially promoting osteogenesis.
source: Alternatively, endogenous collagen may bind α11β1 differently than exogenous collagen, potentially promoting osteogenesis.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential alternative explanation.

claim: It remains untested whether integrin α11 regulates osteogenesis during fetal or early postnatal development.
source: Since Lepr-Cre; Itga11fl/fl mice delete Itga11 in postnatal bone marrow cells that exhibit little contribution to the skeleton prior to two months of age (Zhou et al., 2014), it remains untested whether integrin α11 regulates osteogenesis during fetal or early postnatal development.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study, with citation to prior work.

claim: If integrin α11 regulates osteogenesis during development, this would raise the possibility of a distinct osteogenic ligand for α11 during development as Osteolectin deficient mice do not appear to exhibit defects in skeletal development.
source: If so, this would raise the possibility of a distinct osteogenic ligand for α11 during development as Osteolectin deficient mice do not appear to exhibit defects in skeletal development (Yue et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation about a potential implication, with citation to prior work.

claim: Integrin α11 may have non-osteogenic functions in certain other cell types, or during development, in cells that are not competent to undergo osteogenesis.
source: While integrin α11 is not widely expressed by non-osteogenic cells, integrin α11 may have non-osteogenic functions in certain other cell types, or during development, in cells that are not competent to undergo osteogenesis.
evidence: This is speculation about potential additional functions of integrin α11.

claim: Integrin α11 is expressed by periodontal ligament fibroblasts and is required for the migration of these cells during ligament development, leading to a failure of tooth eruption in germline Itga11 deficient mice.
source: Integrin α11 is expressed by periodontal ligament fibroblasts and is required for the migration of these cells during ligament development, leading to a failure of tooth eruption in germline Itga11 deficient mice (Popova et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Collagen binding to α11β1 may have biologically distinct consequences in cells that are not competent to form bone.
source: This raises the possibility that collagen binding to α11β1 may have biologically distinct consequences in cells that are not competent to form bone.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that α11 has different functions in different cell types.

claim: Integrins can function as mechanosensors.
source: Given that integrins can function as mechanosensors (Schwartz, 2010), our data raise the possibility that integrin α11 mediates the osteogenic response to mechanical loading in bones.
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work on integrins as mechanosensors.

claim: Integrin α11 may mediate the osteogenic response to mechanical loading in bones.
source: Given that integrins can function as mechanosensors (Schwartz, 2010), our data raise the possibility that integrin α11 mediates the osteogenic response to mechanical loading in bones.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known mechanosensory function of integrins and the role of α11 in osteogenesis.

claim: Skeletal stem cells in the developing jaw undergo osteogenesis in response to mechanical forces by activating FAK, suggesting the involvement of integrins in this process.
source: Interestingly, it was recently discovered that skeletal stem cells in the developing jaw undergo osteogenesis in response to mechanical forces by activating FAK, suggesting the involvement of integrins in this process (Ransom et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from recent work.

claim: The identification of a new ligand/receptor pair that regulates the maintenance of the adult skeleton offers the opportunity to better understand the physiological and pathological mechanisms that influence skeletal homeostasis.
source: In conclusion, we identify integrin α11 as an Osteolectin receptor and a new regulator of osteogenesis and adult skeleton maintenance. The identification of a new ligand/receptor pair that regulates the maintenance of the adult skeleton offers the opportunity to better understand the physiological and pathological mechanisms that influence skeletal homeostasis.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: LepR+ bone marrow stromal cells are the major source of osteoblasts and adipocytes in adult mouse bone marrow.
source: Leptin Receptor+ (LepR+) bone marrow stromal cells are the major source of osteoblasts and adipocytes in adult mouse bone marrow (Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: LepR+ cells arise postnatally in the bone marrow, where they are initially rare and make little contribution to the skeleton during development, but expand to account for 0.3% of cells in adult bone marrow.
source: These cells arise postnatally in the bone marrow, where they are initially rare and make little contribution to the skeleton during development, but expand to account for 0.3% of cells in adult bone marrow (Mizoguchi et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Nearly all fibroblast colony-forming cells (CFU-F) in adult mouse bone marrow arise from LepR+ cells.
source: Nearly all fibroblast colony-forming cells (CFU-F) in adult mouse bone marrow arise from these LepR+ cells, and a subset of LepR+ cells form multilineage colonies containing osteoblasts, adipocytes, and chondrocytes, suggesting they are highly enriched for skeletal stem cells (Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: A subset of LepR+ cells form multilineage colonies containing osteoblasts, adipocytes, and chondrocytes, suggesting they are highly enriched for skeletal stem cells.
source: Nearly all fibroblast colony-forming cells (CFU-F) in adult mouse bone marrow arise from these LepR+ cells, and a subset of LepR+ cells form multilineage colonies containing osteoblasts, adipocytes, and chondrocytes, suggesting they are highly enriched for skeletal stem cells (Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: LepR+ cells are a critical source of growth factors that maintain hematopoietic stem cells and other primitive hematopoietic progenitors in bone marrow.
source: LepR+ cells are also a critical source of growth factors that maintain hematopoietic stem cells and other primitive hematopoietic progenitors in bone marrow (Ding and Morrison, 2013; Ding et al., 2012; Himburg et al., 2018; Oguro et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Clec11a is a secreted glycoprotein of the C-type lectin domain superfamily.
source: We discovered that Clec11a, a secreted glycoprotein of the C-type lectin domain superfamily (Bannwarth et al., 1999; Bannwarth et al., 1998), was preferentially expressed by LepR+ cells (Yue et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Clec11a was preferentially expressed by LepR+ cells.
source: We discovered that Clec11a, a secreted glycoprotein of the C-type lectin domain superfamily (Bannwarth et al., 1999; Bannwarth et al., 1998), was preferentially expressed by LepR+ cells (Yue et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Prior studies had observed Clec11a expression in bone marrow but inferred based on colony-forming assays in culture that it was a hematopoietic growth factor.
source: Prior studies had observed Clec11a expression in bone marrow but inferred based on colony-forming assays in culture that it was a hematopoietic growth factor (Hiraoka et al., 1997; Hiraoka et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Osteolectin/Clec11a is not required for normal hematopoiesis.
source: We made germline knockout mice and found it is not required for normal hematopoiesis but that it is required for the maintenance of the adult skeleton (Yue et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Osteolectin/Clec11a deficient mice formed their skeleton normally during development and were otherwise grossly normal as adults but exhibited significantly reduced osteogenesis and bone volume beginning by 2 months of age.
source: The mutant mice formed their skeleton normally during development and were otherwise grossly normal as adults but exhibited significantly reduced osteogenesis and bone volume beginning by 2 months of age (Yue et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Recombinant Osteolectin protein promoted osteogenic differentiation by bone marrow stromal cells in vitro and in vivo.
source: Recombinant protein promoted osteogenic differentiation by bone marrow stromal cells in vitro and in vivo (Yue et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Osteolectin/Clec11a is expressed by a subset of LepR+ stromal cells in the bone marrow as well as by osteoblasts, osteocytes, and hypertrophic chondrocytes.
source: Osteolectin/Clec11a is expressed by a subset of LepR+ stromal cells in the bone marrow as well as by osteoblasts, osteocytes, and hypertrophic chondrocytes.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact from prior work.

claim: The Wnt signaling pathway is a particularly important regulator of osteogenesis, as GSK3 inhibition and β-catenin accumulation promote the differentiation of skeletal stem/progenitor cells into osteoblasts.
source: The Wnt signaling pathway is a particularly important regulator of osteogenesis, as GSK3 inhibition and β-catenin accumulation promote the differentiation of skeletal stem/progenitor cells into osteoblasts (Bennett et al., 2005; Dy et al., 2012; Hernandez et al., 2010; Krishnan et al., 2006; Kulkarni et al., 2006; Rodda and McMahon, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations that promote Wnt pathway activation increase bone mass in humans and in mice.
source: Consistent with this, mutations that promote Wnt pathway activation increase bone mass in humans and in mice (Ai et al., 2005; Balemans et al., 2001; Boyden et al., 2002) while mutations that reduce Wnt pathway activation reduce bone mass in humans and in mice (Gong et al., 2001; Holmen et al., 2004; Kato et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations that reduce Wnt pathway activation reduce bone mass in humans and in mice.
source: Consistent with this, mutations that promote Wnt pathway activation increase bone mass in humans and in mice (Ai et al., 2005; Balemans et al., 2001; Boyden et al., 2002) while mutations that reduce Wnt pathway activation reduce bone mass in humans and in mice (Gong et al., 2001; Holmen et al., 2004; Kato et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The Wnt pathway can be activated by integrin signaling.
source: The Wnt pathway can be activated by integrin signaling.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: There are 18 integrin α subunits and 8 β subunits, forming 24 different functional integrin heterodimer complexes.
source: There are 18 integrin α subunits and 8 β subunits, forming 24 different functional integrin heterodimer complexes (Humphries et al., 2006; Hynes, 1992).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Integrin signaling promotes Wnt pathway activation through Integrin-Linked Kinase (ILK)-mediated phosphorylation of GSK3 and nuclear translocation of β-catenin.
source: Integrin signaling promotes Wnt pathway activation through Integrin-Linked Kinase (ILK)-mediated phosphorylation of GSK3 and nuclear translocation of β-catenin (Burkhalter et al., 2011; Delcommenne et al., 1998; Novak et al., 1998; Rallis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Conditional deletion of Ilk or Ptk2 from osteoblast progenitors reduces osteogenesis and depletes trabecular bone in adult mice.
source: Conditional deletion of Ilk or Ptk2 (which encodes Focal Adhesion Kinase, FAK) from osteoblast progenitors reduces osteogenesis and depletes trabecular bone in adult mice (Dejaeger et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2016), suggesting a role for integrins in adult osteogenesis.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Conditional deletion of β1 integrin from chondrocytes or skeletal stem/progenitor cells impairs chondrocyte function and skeletal ossification during development.
source: Conditional deletion of β1 integrin from chondrocytes or skeletal stem/progenitor cells impairs chondrocyte function and skeletal ossification during development (Aszodi et al., 2003; Raducanu et al., 2009; Shekaran et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Activation of αvβ1 signaling by Osteopontin promotes the osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal progenitors.
source: Activation of αvβ1 signaling by Osteopontin (Chen et al., 2014) or α5β1 signaling by Fibronectin (Hamidouche et al., 2009; Moursi et al., 1997) promotes the osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal progenitors.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Activation of α5β1 signaling by Fibronectin promotes the osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal progenitors.
source: Activation of αvβ1 signaling by Osteopontin (Chen et al., 2014) or α5β1 signaling by Fibronectin (Hamidouche et al., 2009; Moursi et al., 1997) promotes the osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal progenitors.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Germline deletion of integrin α10 leads to defects in chondrocyte proliferation and growth plate function.
source: Germline deletion of integrin α10 leads to defects in chondrocyte proliferation and growth plate function (Bengtsson et al., 2005) and germline deletion of integrin α11 leads to defects in tooth development (Popova et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Germline deletion of integrin α11 leads to defects in tooth development.
source: Germline deletion of integrin α10 leads to defects in chondrocyte proliferation and growth plate function (Bengtsson et al., 2005) and germline deletion of integrin α11 leads to defects in tooth development (Popova et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Little is known about which integrins are required for adult osteogenesis in vivo.
source: However, little is known about which integrins are required for adult osteogenesis in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: The Osteolectin/Clec11a gene first appeared in bony fish and is conserved among bony vertebrates.
source: The Osteolectin/Clec11a gene first appeared in bony fish and is conserved among bony vertebrates (Yue et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior work.

claim: Osteolectin contains a glutamic acid-rich sequence, an alpha-helical leucine zipper, and a C-type lectin domain.
source: Osteolectin contains a glutamic acid-rich sequence, an alpha-helical leucine zipper, and a C-type lectin domain (Figure 1A and B) (Bannwarth et al., 1999; Bannwarth et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work and shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Integrin α11 is expressed by human bone marrow stromal cells in a way that correlates with osteogenic potential in culture.
source: Consistent with our results, integrin α11 is expressed by human bone marrow stromal cells in a way that correlates with osteogenic potential in culture (Kaltz et al., 2010); however, α11 is not known to regulate osteogenesis.
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Integrin α11 heterodimerizes with integrin β1.
source: Integrin α11 heterodimerizes with integrin β1 (Velling et al., 1999) and the only known ligand for α11β1 is collagen (Popova et al., 2004; Velling et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The only known ligand for α11β1 is collagen.
source: Integrin α11 heterodimerizes with integrin β1 (Velling et al., 1999) and the only known ligand for α11β1 is collagen (Popova et al., 2004; Velling et al., 1999).

claim: Few cells express integrin α11, and it has been studied less than other integrins.
